subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 12 of Year 4 Computing at Ehel Academy — the very last unit of the year. Be an Artist. But there is no paper and no paintbrush: the canvas is a tiny computer called the micro:bit, and the paint is light. The micro:bit has 25 little red lights — LEDs — in a 5-by-5 grid. By turning those lights on and off, we can draw a square, a heart, a diamond, an arrow, or our own repeating pattern, like the geometric tile-work in a mosaic. the artistic title hides a serious computing idea: physical computing. A micro:bit is a physical computing device — a small computer that senses the world and acts on it. It takes in inputs (a button press, a touch, a shake) and gives out outputs (a shape of light, a sound). The big idea is that we can program different outputs from different inputs: Button A shows a square, Button B shows a heart, touching the gold logo plays a twinkle sound. The repeat ( ) loop repeats a set number of times and then stops (a count-controlled loop, met earlier this year); the forever loop repeats over and over and never stops. A flashing dot, a twinkling pattern, a blinking arrow — all are loops at work. You also make their art move, using two kinds of loop — blocks that repeat other blocks. And as always, you write the algorithm first (a simple plan) and only then build the code, because a good artist and a good programmer both plan before they start.

outcomes: Explain that a micro:bit is a physical computing device — a small computer that senses the world and acts on it.
Tell the difference between an input (information going into the device, like a button press) and an output (information coming out, like a shape of light or a sound).
Name some inputs on the micro:bit (Button A, Button B, the touch logo, shake) and some outputs (the LED display, the speaker).
Draw a shape or pattern on the 5-by-5 LED grid using the show leds, show icon and show arrow blocks in MakeCode.
Develop an algorithm (a plan) so that different inputs produce different outputs, then build it as a program.
Build a program with a count-controlled loop (the repeat ( ) block) to flash art a set number of times.
Build a program with a forever loop to make art animate over and over.
Test a program part by part, and find and fix (debug) simple mistakes.

Before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already follow, understand and edit algorithms that use repetition, test different parts of a program, and know about count-controlled and forever loops (met earlier in Year 4). They will also have met the micro:bit and its inputs and outputs in Unit 8, "Be an innovator". A quick recap of "input, output, loop" at the start of Session 1 is usually enough.

concepts.title: Our canvas of light (unplugged)
concepts.explanation: A micro:bit is a physical computing device — a tiny computer that senses the world and acts on it. It has inputs (ways for information to go in) and outputs (ways for information to come out). Its main output is the LED display: 25 little red lights, called LEDs, in a 5-by-5 grid. That grid is our canvas, and we paint by choosing which lights are on. An input is something going in; an output is something coming out. Point around the room: a switch is an input, the bulb lighting up is the output; you knock (input) and the door opens (output).
concepts.example: Find one real example of our canvas of light around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you colour a grid to make a recognisable shape? Can you notice symmetry — that a pattern can be balanced left-to-right and top-to-bottom?

concepts.title: Painting shapes with light (outputs) in MakeCode
concepts.explanation: Today we open MakeCode and make our first outputs. We meet four Basic blocks: show icon (a ready-made picture, like a heart or a diamond), show leds (a grid we colour in ourselves to draw our own art), clear screen (turn all the lights off) and pause (ms) (wait for a moment). We also meet show arrow for pointing arrows. On the projector, go to makecode.microbit.org and click New Project. Drag a show icon block into on start and pick the heart from its dropdown — the simulator lights it up at once. Here is a diamond-star pattern to build together (# is a light on. is a light off)
concepts.example: Find one real example of painting shapes with light (outputs) in MakeCode around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that clear screen only turns the lights off — it does not delete your code? Can you open a new project and find the Basic blocks?

concepts.title: Different outputs from different inputs
concepts.explanation:
This is the heart of the unit. We use input blocks so that different inputs make different outputs. From the Input group we meet on button A pressed, on button B pressed, on logo pressed (the gold touch logo) and on shake. Whatever blocks we put inside an input block only run when that input happens.

First, plan. Only then build it.
concepts.example: Drag on button A pressed from Input and drop a show icon (small square) inside; do the same for Button B with a heart, and for on logo pressed add play sound twinkle until done from the Music blocks. It looks like this
concepts.checkYourself: Can you test each input in turn on the simulator, and fix it if an output is on the wrong input? Can you put an output block inside an input block?

concepts.title: Count-controlled loops: flash it a set number of times
concepts.explanation:
Now we make our art repeat. The repeat ( ) block is a count-controlled loop: it repeats the blocks inside it a set number of times and then stops.

How could we make one light blink five times? From the Loops group, drag repeat (5) and build a blink inside it: show one light, wait, clear, wait. Because 1000 ms is 1 second, this blinks on for a second and off for a second, five times, and then stops on its own
concepts.example: Find one real example of count-controlled loops: flash it a set number of times around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you change the number and predict the result? Can you understand that the loop stops on its own after counting? Can you drag a repeat block and put blocks inside its mouth?

concepts.title: Be an artist: forever loops and the light-art show
concepts.explanation: The second loop is forever: it repeats over and over and never stops on its own. It is perfect for art that twinkles or animates. We also compare the two loops — when do we want to stop after a set number (count-controlled), and when do we want it to keep going (forever)? From the Loops group, drag a forever block. Build an animation inside it — an arrow that blinks on and off — and let it run. It never stops until you press the stop button on the simulator
concepts.example: Do it yourself: be an artist: forever loops and the light-art show. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you combine inputs and a loop into one program and test it in parts? Can you build a forever loop and run and stop it?

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work

selfAssessment: I can explain that a micro:bit is a physical computing device — a small computer that senses the world and acts on it.
I can tell the difference between an input (information going into the device, like a button press) and an output (information coming out, like a shape of light or a sound).
I can name some inputs on the micro:bit (Button A, Button B, the touch logo, shake) and some outputs (the LED display, the speaker).
I can draw a shape or pattern on the 5-by-5 LED grid using the show leds, show icon and show arrow blocks in MakeCode.
I can develop an algorithm (a plan) so that different inputs produce different outputs, then build it as a program.
I can build a program with a count-controlled loop (the repeat ( ) block) to flash art a set number of times.
I can build a program with a forever loop to make art animate over and over.
I can test a program part by part, and find and fix (debug) simple mistakes.

I can before this unit (from the syllabus), children should already follow, understand and edit algorithms that use repetition, test different parts of a program, and know about count-controlled and forever loops (met earlier in Year 4). They will also have met the micro:bit and its inputs and outputs in Unit 8, "Be an innovator". A quick recap of "input, output, loop" at the start of Session 1 is usually enough.
